<div class="eyebrow dark">ABOUT</div>

# I work at the intersection of analytics, research, systems, and implementation.

I am a data and analytics consultant with more than 15 years of experience building analytic products, workforce models, research programs, dashboards, and decision-support systems for government, healthcare, associations, nonprofits, and consulting clients.

The recurring theme in my work is translating an ambiguous organizational problem into something concrete: a research question, a data strategy, a model, a dashboard, a workflow, or a system that people can actually use.

## Background

Most recently I served as **Director of Health Workforce Consulting at GlobalData**, leading complex analytics engagements for state agencies, hospital associations, professional societies, and federal clients. My work included workforce projection methods, reusable R/Shiny dashboard frameworks, validation and documentation systems, and a DuckDB + object-storage proof of concept for lower-friction analytic architecture.

Before that, I helped establish Utah's legislatively created **Health Workforce Information Center** and spent more than a decade at the **Utah Medical Education Council**, where I led statewide research programs covering multiple health professions and built survey, modeling, reporting, data-integration, cloud-hosted analytics, and public R/Shiny capabilities.

Earlier public-sector and nonprofit work gave me practical experience with programs, policy, operations, grants, administrative systems, and direct service. That experience still shapes how I approach analytics: the data system is never separate from the people, workflows, institutions, and decisions around it.

## How I think about consulting

::: {.principle-grid}
::: {.principle}
### Understand the decision before designing the analysis
A technically elegant answer to the wrong question is still the wrong answer.
:::
::: {.principle}
### Stakeholder input is part of system design
Usability, trust, incentives, workflow, and implementation constraints should shape the solution from the beginning.
:::
::: {.principle}
### Prefer maintainable over impressive
The right architecture is the one the organization can understand, afford, validate, and sustain.
:::
::: {.principle}
### Analysis is not finished when the model runs
Interpretation, communication, implementation, documentation, and handoff are part of the analytic product.
:::
:::

## Education and perspective

I hold four degrees from the **University of Utah**: an MBA with a Certificate in Information Systems, an MPA focused on Program Evaluation and Policy Analysis, a B.A. in Political Science with a Certificate in International Relations, and a B.A. in Spanish.

My professional work has crossed public policy, healthcare, labor and workforce analysis, program evaluation, data science, analytics engineering, and technical product delivery. I have also served as a peer reviewer, federal grant reviewer, nursing workforce center board president, and Salt Lake City planning commissioner and commission chair.

One project that strongly influenced how I think about analytics implementation was an **IBM Health Corps** collaboration focused on modeling primary-care workforce needs. The technical analysis mattered, but so did stakeholder participation, system design, usability, and the practical question of how a new analytic approach would be deployed and used.
